title: 60,000 Migrants Overwhelm Ceuta as Italy Suspends Schengen With Spain, Hamas Disarmament Deal Faces Israeli Resistance
subhead: A mass crossing from Morocco into Spain's Ceuta enclave triggers Europe's biggest migration crisis in years, while Hamas agrees to disarm but Israel balks, and Trump retreats on Patriot missiles for Ukraine.

sections.heading: Ceuta Migration Crisis: 60,000 Cross, 57 Dead, Schengen Fractures
sections.body:
As many as 60,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in roughly 24 hours, overwhelming a city of 85,000 residents and creating the largest single-day migration event in Europe in recent memory. At least 57 people drowned attempting the crossing, according to the Guardian and BBC. Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called it 'a violation of Spain's territorial integrity' and blamed human traffickers for spreading false narratives about open borders.

By Friday evening, Spanish authorities said approximately 48,000 migrants had voluntarily returned to Morocco, with no viable onward route to mainland Spain or the EU. But the political damage was immediate: Italy announced it was temporarily suspending its Schengen free-movement arrangements with Spain by air and sea, instituting targeted checks on third-country nationals arriving from Spain. Several other EU states called for broader suspensions of Spain's Schengen membership. The crisis has exposed deep fractures in Europe's border regime and placed Madrid's pro-immigration government under intense domestic pressure.
sections.whyItMatters: The Ceuta crossing is the largest single migration event to hit a European border in years, and Italy's Schengen suspension sets a precedent that could reshape free movement within the EU. The speed with which the political response shifted from humanitarian concern to border lockdown reveals how fragile Europe's migration consensus remains.

sections.heading: Hamas Disarmament Deal Signed — But Israel Hasn't Agreed
sections.body:
Hamas confirmed on Thursday it has accepted a phased disarmament plan brokered through the US-led Board of Peace. Under the deal, Hamas would inventory and store its heavy weapons — including remaining rockets, military production sites, and tunnels — under the supervision of a Palestinian National Committee and an International Stabilisation Force. Personal arms and police weapons would be registered and gradually transferred to a new Palestinian police force. Israeli forces would withdraw incrementally to the agreed Yellow Line, with a 24-hour deadline for initial pullback once Israel approves the plan.

The gap between the announcement and reality remains vast. Israel has not signed on. Far-right Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called the plan 'unacceptable,' and Israeli officials insist no withdrawal will occur before Hamas is fully disarmed. Meanwhile, the Israeli military has expanded its control beyond the original Yellow Line, now occupying more than 60% of Gaza. Trump claimed at Camp David that Israel was 'very happy' with the deal, but declined to say whether disarmament or withdrawal would come first. On the ground in Gaza, reaction was muted — after years of failed ceasefires, few residents expressed optimism. Over 1,168 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli strikes since the October ceasefire began, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first time Hamas has formally agreed to disarm, which is a significant shift. But Israel's refusal to commit, the lack of a sequencing mechanism, and the reality of expanded Israeli territorial control mean the deal could easily stall — or collapse entirely.

sections.heading: Trump Backtracks on Patriot Missiles for Ukraine as Kyiv Comes Under Fire
sections.body:
At Camp David on Friday, Donald Trump walked back his suggestion — made just weeks ago at a NATO summit in Turkey — that Ukraine could be licensed to produce Patriot interceptor missiles domestically. 'We have not agreed to that,' Trump told reporters. 'It's a hard thing to give away that kind of technology. People that you give that technology, they can some day turn on you.' The reversal came hours after Russia launched more than 70 missiles and 280 drones at Ukraine overnight, killing at least eight people — including five members of the Voronov family, whose home near Kryvyi Rih was destroyed by a ballistic missile. Three of their children remain missing. In Kyiv, at least four people were killed in a separate strike early Saturday.

Poland confirmed that a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile landed in a field in eastern Poland, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk stating it was likely newly manufactured — 'produced near Moscow in the second quarter of this year' — evidence that Russia is burning through newly built stock rather than relying on aging reserves. Poland summoned the Russian ambassador in protest. Meanwhile, Zelenskyy has been pushing Trump to approve the use of Starlink for guiding Ukrainian strikes inside Russia, a request Trump did not grant. Thousands of Ukrainians protested in Kyiv over Zelenskyy's dismissal of Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, a figure widely credited with driving military innovation during the war.
sections.whyItMatters: Trump's reversal on Patriot production cuts off Ukraine's best path to sustainable air defense at a moment when Russia is escalating bombardment. The Polish missile strike — and confirmation it was newly manufactured — underscores that Russia's war economy is producing weapons faster than Western stockpiles can be replenished.

sections.heading: Iran Strikes Tankers Under US Escort as Hormuz Stays Blocked
sections.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said it struck two oil tankers attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz under US military escort on Friday, while four other vessels turned back. The IRGC claimed the ships were using an 'undeclared route' through the southern strait near Oman. The strait has been nearly closed to commercial traffic for two weeks since fighting between Iran and the US resumed, keeping oil prices elevated — crude pushed past $90 a barrel on Thursday after US strikes on Iran in retaliation for attacks on its Jordan bases.

Trump convened his cabinet at Camp David to discuss the war's trajectory, five months after promising the campaign would last weeks. A Reuters-Ipsos poll this week found only one in three Americans now supports the war, the lowest level since it began. The Senate narrowly rejected a war powers resolution to discontinue the conflict, voting 49-50. Energy companies continue to post record profits: ExxonMobil's profits doubled and Chevron reported more than five times its profits from the same period last year. Kuwait's defence ministry reported shooting down Iranian drones targeting military facilities without casualties. Iran also launched drones at US forces in Kuwait, though the US Defense Department said there was no major impact on its bases.
sections.whyItMatters: The Hormuz standoff has become a war of attrition with no exit strategy. Trump faces mounting domestic pressure over gas prices and a war he promised would be short, while Iran's ability to disrupt global energy shipping remains undiminished. The profit surge by energy companies adds a politically volatile dimension to the conflict's economic fallout.

sections.heading: US Treasury Revealed Buying Yen as Global Markets Rattle
sections.body:
A Reuters photograph captured Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's handwritten to-do list during the Camp David cabinet meeting, revealing a plan to 'Buy Japanese Yen (JPY) $5-10 bil.' The notepad was visible during the televised portion of the meeting. Two hours earlier, the Treasury had notified banks it might intervene in the yen market. Japanese authorities separately intervened to prop up the yen, which had dropped to its weakest level since 1986, driven partly by rising oil prices from the Hormuz disruption.

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York subsequently sold euros to buy yen on behalf of the Treasury Department, the Financial Times reported, marking the first US currency intervention to support the yen since the coordinated G7 action after Japan's 2011 earthquake. The dollar dropped from about 158.9 yen to 157.6 yen within an hour in late-afternoon trading. The inadvertent disclosure has raised questions about whether the intervention was planned in coordination with Japan or represented a unilateral US response to currency pressures amplified by the Iran conflict's effect on energy prices.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first US yen intervention in 15 years, and the accidental disclosure of Bessent's notes is a remarkable breach of financial protocol. It signals that the US-Iran conflict's economic ripple effects have reached the point where Washington is deploying direct currency tools, and it raises the question of how much of US macro policy is now being driven by war-driven energy inflation.

sections.heading: Super El Niño Threatens India's Monsoon as UN Warns Planet Is 'On Fire'
sections.body:
The World Meteorological Organization warned on Friday that a strengthening El Niño system is pushing global weather into 'uncharted territory,' with Pacific waters warmer than any previous El Niño at this stage. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the phenomenon was 'adding fuel to a planet already on fire.' Marine heatwaves are intensifying, with sea surface temperatures likely to exceed 2.9°C above normal in multiple regions.

The forecast poses a direct threat to India's monsoon, with the WMO giving an 'enhanced probability for below-normal rainfall' across the Indian Ocean basin — a pattern that would devastate agricultural output and food security for over a billion people. Southern Europe, already battling devastating wildfires across France, Spain, Portugal, Greece, and Turkey, faces above-average rainfall even as drought conditions persist elsewhere. In France, investigators found that officials failed to enforce wildfire buffer-zone regulations in areas hit by the country's worst fires in decades. Over 200,000 hectares have burned in Spain this year — five times the seasonal average.
sections.whyItMatters: The combination of a supercharged El Niño and ongoing climate disruption means the second half of 2026 is likely to see compounding extremes — drought in South Asia, flooding in southern Europe, and wildfire conditions across the Mediterranean — all layered on top of the economic disruption already caused by the Iran conflict and the war in Ukraine.

bottomLine: August 1 marks a day when multiple crises converged: the largest single-day migration event into Europe in years exposed the fragility of the Schengen system, Hamas signed a disarmament deal that Israel has not accepted, Trump reversed his promise on Patriot missiles for Ukraine even as Russian missiles killed civilians and struck NATO territory in Poland, Iran continued to strangle Hormuz while facing no viable path to de-escalation, and the US accidentally revealed a historic currency intervention driven by war inflation. Meanwhile, the WMO's super El Niño warning adds a slow-moving global catastrophe to an already overloaded agenda. The connective thread across all of these stories: existing systems — borders, ceasefires, alliances, currency regimes, climate patterns — are being tested simultaneously, and none of them are holding firm.
